remit

corroboration
Independent evidence supporting a claim.

An operation undoing a previous transaction.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The first comparison of the recovered authorisations book produced a result that was promising precisely because it was limited. Several reference numbers corresponded to entries in the trust's surviving payment-exceptions material. The overlap supported the volume's connection to the 2011 student travel scheme; it could not certify the authenticity of every page or establish the execution of any particular authorisation.

Fiona Bell described a clearer copy of the delegated-authority rules. Certain exceptions fell within a finance manager's remit, while requests above a specified threshold required referral to the trust chair. The amount defining that threshold remained partly illegible. Moreover, the initials beside several entries in the recovered book had not been matched to verified staff signatures.

“Malcolm Vale held the chair's position,” Sarah observed. “Surely that narrows it down.”

“It narrows down who might have had authority,” Emma replied. “It tells us nothing reliable about who wrote those initials.”

The trust was consulting contemporaneous personnel records before attributing an entry to an individual. Emma knew how seductive a familiar name could become when placed beside an unexplained mark. She was determined not to turn a hypothesis into an allegation.

Another document introduced a different kind of evidence: a monthly summary of payments submitted to the bank. It contained aggregate figures, but Fiona could not yet provide verified links between those totals and the authorisations in the book. An instruction to pay, an accounting summary and proof that an intended recipient received funds were related propositions, not interchangeable ones.

Emma returned briefly to the letter shown by Helen Ward. Its selection language and conditions were clear, but the copy had not been fully authenticated and no corresponding transfer had been established. She would not use confidential student data to manufacture a link between an unnamed family and an unidentified entry.

The physical examination offered a smaller, corrective discovery. The leaf previously described as loose remained attached along a narrow edge. Inspectors found no evidence of a sheet missing at that point. It would have been misleading to continue speaking of a page that had been removed. Emma amended her notes rather than preserving the more dramatic possibility.

Fiona agreed to ask for a separate review of the authorisation entries against staffing information and available banking material. She made no promise of complete reconciliation. A decade and a half of fragmented recordkeeping might prevent any definitive account of some transactions.

At the end of the afternoon Fiona reported a possible bridge between two sets of records. A follow-up reference attached to one exception entry appeared again in a banking index. The underlying entry had not been inspected. The code might refer to an attempted transfer, an adjustment, a reversal or a successfully completed payment. Its repetition established a traceable lead, not its meaning.

Sarah was eager to describe the first confirmed irregularity. Emma stopped her.

“A matching code is not an irregularity. We don't know what the bank did.”

She recorded three findings: selected reference numbers matched; the initials remained unattributed; and the bank index contained one potentially related reference whose transaction status was unknown.

As dusk settled over Edinburgh, she looked again at the final code. Unlike the vague warnings and incomplete figures that had occupied so much of the investigation, it posed a question that a specific document might answer. Its answer, however, belonged to the final stage of the inquiry, not to Emma's imagination.
